whyCorrect: The stated goal is to contrast the subject matter of the two prints, which means what each print depicts, not how it was made or when. Go back to the notes and pull only the two bullets that describe content: Andrews's Hyde Park shows a tranquil, everyday scene, and Tana's Amanzi Amthatha shows an explicitly political scene of a Xhosa warrior fighting colonial rule. Choice B puts exactly those two facts side by side and joins them with "while," so the contrast is between the images themselves. Every other choice contrasts something real from the notes, but not the subject matter.

whyWrong.A: This contrasts printing technique, not subject matter, and the contrast is false on top of that: the notes say lino cutting is a type of relief printing, so calling one a linocut and the other a relief print sets up a difference that does not exist.
whyWrong.C: This contrasts the dates the prints were made. The years are accurate from the notes, but a date is not what a work depicts, so it does not meet the stated goal.
whyWrong.D: This describes the carving-and-stamping process the two works share, then repeats the same false linocut-versus-relief distinction as choice A. It is about method throughout and never mentions what either print shows.

commonMistakes: Picking whichever choice contains the word "contrast" or a "however"; the connector is not the test, the two things being compared are.
tips: Underline the noun in the goal sentence (here, "subject matter") and reject any choice whose two halves are not both about that noun.

whyCorrect: The goal has two parts joined by "and": introduce Reginald Fessenden and say what he is known for. A choice has to do both, so treat it as a two-item checklist and cross off any choice that misses either half. Choice B introduces him (an electronic communications specialist who worked for Edison) and then states what he is best known for (pioneering the radio technology behind the first transmission of speech by radio), which is the second bullet about him. It also keeps Fessenden as the grammatical subject, so he is the person being introduced rather than a detail inside someone else's story.

whyWrong.A: This does the introducing half only. It gives his specialty and his employer but never mentions radio, so the "what he is known for" half of the goal goes unaddressed.
whyWrong.C: This makes Thomas Edison the subject and reduces Fessenden to one name in a list of employees. It uses accurate notes, but it introduces Edison's working method, not Fessenden, and never says what Fessenden is known for.
whyWrong.D: This is about Frank J. Sprague and electric traction. It answers the goal for the wrong person entirely, and Fessenden is not mentioned at all.

commonMistakes: Stopping at the first choice that names Fessenden correctly; choice A is true and on topic but satisfies only half of a two-part goal.
tips: Split a goal sentence at its "and" into two requirements and check each choice against both before comparing choices to each other.
